blind_target.evidence_quote: Examining self-reported reservation wages from the 1979-80 waves of the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (NLSY), Holzer concludes that 26 to 42 percent of the race difference in the length of jobless spells is due to the higher wages sought by young Black men. This replication uses NLSY reservation wage data from 1979 through 1986.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Thus, evidence from the NLSY does not support the claim that reservation wage differences explain the race employment gap.

blind_target.evidence_quote: MacKuen, Erikson, and Stimson (1989, 1992) argue that the aggregate distribution of party identification, or macropartisanship, shifts significantly over short periods in response to changes in presidential popularity and consumer sentiment. We replicate this analysis using a more extensive inventory of Gallup and CBS/New York Timesdata and find considerably less evidence of partisan fluctuation.
blind_target.outcome_quote: The amount of partisan change caused by short-term movements in consumer sentiment and presidential popularity is found to be two to three times smaller than initially reported by MacKuen et al. (1989). Our results indicate that macropartisanship adjusts to short-term shocks in a limited and gradual fashion, consistent with traditional views of partisan realignment.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The abstract describes both cited originals as reporting responsiveness to these inputs and reports responsiveness in the same direction but smaller. Reduced magnitude alone does not imply mixed. Full-text verdict and reference entries unavailable.

prior_decision.quote: MacKuen, Erikson, and Stimson (1989, 1992) argue that the aggregate distribution of party identification, or macropartisanship, shifts significantly over short periods in response to changes in presidential popularity and consumer sentiment. Their results are based on a subset of Gallup surveys available from 1953 to 1988 and only those CBS/New York Timessurveys conducted during the Reagan administration. We replicate this analysis using a more extensive inventory of Gallup and CBS/New York Timesdata and find considerably less evidence of partisan fluctuation. The amount of partisan change caused by short-term movements in consumer sentiment and presidential popularity is found to be two to three times smaller than initially reported by MacKuen et al. (1989).
prior_decision.reason: The abstract jointly cites MacKuen, Erikson, and Stimson (1989, 1992) before referring to '[t]heir results' and stating '[w]e replicate this analysis', while explicitly quantifying the comparison only against MacKuen et al. (1989). Because only the abstract is available and the full text and reference list are unseen, the supplied source neither establishes that the 1992 study is independently re-tested nor proves its exclusion from the full-text replication.
